$comment: Rendering ceilings for the four primary flows: the Overview, the runs list, run
detail and quarantine. A **baseline**, not a live observation — `pnpm test:render`
measures a real browser and compares against this.
The shape is the ratchet the repository already uses for coverage and complexity:
a floor is recorded once, deliberately and by hand, and thereafter only a
regression fails. That is what keeps the gate from being turned off — a gate whose
own threshold can be rewritten in the same commit is a gate that agrees with the
tree instead of the code. `render:baseline` is `never-in-ci` in gate-tooling.json
for exactly that reason.
`recorded: false` is a MEASUREMENT phase, not a failing one, and the distinction is
enforced rather than documented. `scripts/lib/render-gate-phase.mjs` derives the tier
`test:render` is allowed to have from this file, and `gate-tooling.test.mjs` fails until
`scripts/gate-tooling.json` agrees. So:
- `recorded: false` -> the CI job measures the four routes, publishes the numbers to
the job summary, compares nothing, and is tiered `pr-reporting` — not a required
check. A required check that can never pass blocks every pull request and teaches
reviewers to ignore red.
- `recorded: true`  -> the same spec compares against these ceilings and fails on a
regression, and `test:render` must be `pr-blocking`. Leaving it below that is a
real gate nobody is required to satisfy, which is the worse state.
Graduating is therefore one commit with two parts: record a real run, and raise the
tier. The test refuses to pass if only one of them happened, so `recorded: true`
beside invented numbers cannot quietly become a gate that is green and unenforced.
Why the budget has to exist before the effect does: `backdrop-filter` repaints the
backdrop on every frame, and the whole of the glass argument is about that cost. The
budget therefore has two halves and they are not the same kind of number:
- `lcpMs`/`inpMs`/`cls`/`longTasks` are TIMINGS. They need reference hardware, so
they are null and uncompared, and `recorded` stays false.
- `glassStackDepth` is a STRUCTURAL CEILING. It is not a timing and does not depend
on hardware — it is how deeply translucent surfaces nest on that route, which is a
property of the component tree rather than of the data. It is compared in every
phase, including this one, because a budget that ships an unmeasured cost is the
defect `RF-9` records. Adding glass without it would have been adding compositing
work to four routes under a gate that watches none of it.
**Depth, not a total, and the first run showed why.** Counting every element with a
computed `backdrop-filter` gave 10 on `/dashboard/runs` and 2 on `/dashboard/quarantine`
with one run seeded — the route has one card per row. A ceiling of 10 would have been a
statement about how many runs existed when the budget was written, and the dashboard
would have failed its own budget when a second run landed. Depth cannot grow with a row
count, so it is a constraint the design can hold. Depth is also the closer cost proxy: a
translucent panel samples everything painted behind it, so two stacked panels composite
roughly four times the area of one.
The count is of *elements with a computed `backdrop-filter`*, not of elements carrying
a glass class, so a token that stops applying stops counting.
**The ceiling is 0 on every route since the flat redesign.** The product ships no
translucent surface at all, so any element with a computed `backdrop-filter` is a
regression this spec reports by route. The depth counter is kept rather than deleted
because a ban that nothing measures in a real browser is a ban on paper.
How to populate it: run `pnpm render:baseline` on the reference hardware the plan's
D10 commits to, which writes the measured values here with `recorded: true` and the
date. Review the diff before committing it — the point of recording the number once is
that the next change has to beat it. A GitHub runner is not that hardware: the
ceilings describe a self-hosted single-node install, so a run there would record the
wrong number just as honestly as a guess would.
reason: Never measured. Every timing ceiling below is null because no run on the reference hardware has populated it, so the timing half of this budget currently protects nothing. This is the same defect the ledger records as RF-9 for performance/thresholds.json, adopted here deliberately so the rendering budget does not ship as an unvalidated estimate — except that this file refuses to pretend. The timings stay null and the gate stays in its measurement phase rather than being given numbers that mean nothing. Populate with `pnpm render:baseline` on the reference hardware the plan's D10 commits to, and raise `test:render` to `pr-blocking` in the same commit. Tracked as PERF-1. The `glassStackDepth` ceilings are the exception: they are not timings, they are 0 because the plane is flat, and they are compared today.

/dashboard.$why: The Overview: the first paint a person sees, and the screen that answers "can I ship". It replaced /login, which no longer exists (ADR-006). Opaque like everything else, so the glass depth is 0.

/dashboard/runs.$why: The runs list. The heaviest of the four: every row is a run, and a slow one here is a dashboard that appears to hang. Opaque rows on an opaque plane, so the glass depth is 0.

/dashboard/runs/:runId.$why: Where a person decides whether a release is safe, so a rendering defect here is the most expensive one in the product. Evidence is never read through a translucent surface: the glass depth is 0.

/dashboard/quarantine.$why: The filter surface, and the only primary flow whose content changes on every keystroke — so its INP is the reading most likely to catch an unthrottled re-render. Opaque, glass depth 0.
